paragraphs: Recognizing an object from an unfamiliar angle raises a question about visual memory: can people succeed by comparing flat images, or do they use information about three-dimensional structure? The paper examines whether stronger two-dimensional matching models can explain human performance. Familiarity with particular images clearly matters, but that alone does not establish that recognition relies entirely on stored pictures.

The authors compare human observers with generalized radial basis function models, nearest-neighbor matching that permits affine image transformations, and a Bayesian estimator that integrates over those transformations. These transformations allow more flexibility than simply rotating a template within the image plane. The Bayesian model supplies an optimal reference within the specified family of independent templates and affine transformations.

Relative to each model, humans perform better on unfamiliar views than on familiar template views. This points to stronger generalization in human recognition. Because even the optimal estimator has this relative weakness, the findings challenge the whole tested model family rather than merely one implementation. They do not identify a unique alternative representation.
neurips-1997-2d-observers-for-human-3d-o.tldr: Human recognition of unfamiliar object views challenges models based on independent two-dimensional templates and affine matching.

paragraphs: This paper describes an inexpensive motorized video system that learns to follow a person's head. Its central challenge is deciding which visual evidence remains trustworthy as the surroundings change. A moving object in the background, for example, makes motion alone an unreliable guide to the target.

A convolutional neural network combines normalized brightness and color images with motion information obtained from differences between video frames. It also receives subsampled images, which help it handle changes in the head's apparent size. Training signals come either from real-time graphical input supplied by a user or from an auxiliary infrared detector. These signals guide the network toward the intended target.

During online training, the network rapidly changes the weights assigned to its input channels according to their reliability in the current environment. The reported outcome is robust head tracking despite clutter and other moving objects. The useful design principle is adaptive combination of several visual cues: the system can change which information it emphasizes as conditions change.
neurips-1997-a-neural-network-based-head.tldr: A motorized head tracker learns to combine brightness, color, and motion cues while adapting to their changing reliability.

paragraphs: Regularization discourages large fitted weights and can improve predictions on unseen data. This paper asks how to analyze that improvement precisely, using one-dimensional linear regression with a quadratic penalty, also called ridge regression. The deliberately simple setting makes it possible to study the strength of the penalty and its consequences mathematically.

The analysis treats the inputs as random and allows the fitted linear model to be misspecified, meaning that the underlying relationship need not belong to the chosen model family. The authors derive asymptotic expansions for the optimal regularization parameter and the improvement it produces. Such expansions describe behavior as the amount of data grows, retaining detail needed to distinguish regularized from unregularized fitting.

The paper argues that the asymptotic distribution of the fitted weight alone is insufficient for assessing these benefits. It also constructs examples in which the best choice is no regularization. The result makes the value of regularization a question about the statistical setting, rather than an automatic consequence of adding a penalty.
neurips-1997-asymptotic-theory-for-regul.tldr: A refined analysis of one-dimensional ridge regression characterizes optimal regularization and shows that no penalty can sometimes be best.

paragraphs: EEG recordings mix brain activity with interference from eye movements, blinking, muscles, the heart, and electrical line noise. Discarding contaminated segments loses information. Removing an eye-recording reference through regression also poses a problem: that reference contains some brain activity, so subtracting its contribution removes relevant signal along with interference.

The paper proposes an extended independent component analysis method to separate these contributions. Its model treats the recordings as linear mixtures of independent sources. The extension accommodates both sub-Gaussian and super-Gaussian source distributions, broadening the kinds of statistical patterns the separation algorithm can handle. This provides a common approach to several artifact types rather than requiring an eye-activity reference for each one.

The reported results show effective detection, separation, and removal of varied artifacts, with favorable comparisons to regression methods. The significance is the possibility of cleaning recordings without rejecting every affected segment. The linear-mixture and independent-source assumptions are central to the approach: they specify how the method interprets the recorded channels and separates their contributions.
neurips-1997-extended-ica-removes-artifa.tldr: Extended independent component analysis separates varied EEG artifacts by modeling recordings as linear mixtures of independent sources.

paragraphs: A decision tree's number of leaves is a simple measure of complexity, but it may exaggerate how much of the tree the data actually use. This paper develops generalization bounds that capture that distinction. Its starting point is a set of techniques for thresholded real-valued classifiers whose guarantees can be smaller than conventional bounds based on VC theory.

The authors extend these techniques by expressing Boolean functions as two-layer neural networks built from thresholded convex combinations of Boolean functions. For a tree that correctly classifies its training examples and has bounded depth, the resulting bound uses an effective number of leaves. This quantity becomes smaller when training examples are distributed unevenly across the leaves.

The guarantee also reflects the training sample size, tree depth, and complexity of the functions used at decision nodes. Thus, nominal tree size alone does not determine the bound. The authors obtain related results for disjunctive normal form formulas. Their contribution is theoretical: data-dependent use of a classifier's structure can support sharper error guarantees.
neurips-1997-generalization-in-decision-.tldr: Generalization bounds for decision trees and DNF formulas can reflect effective structural complexity rather than nominal size alone.

paragraphs: This paper improves continuous speech recognition by adding a learned feature-processing stage to an existing continuous hidden Markov model system. The neural network serves as a preprocessor: it transforms acoustic information into features designed to help the underlying recognizer distinguish speech patterns. The architecture therefore preserves the HMM's role while changing the information it receives.

The network takes several frames of feature vectors as input, allowing its output to depend on a short sequence rather than an isolated frame. Its purpose is to make those outputs more discriminative for the particular HMM system. The architecture permits an arbitrary neural network, making the contribution a general way to connect neural feature extraction with continuous HMM recognition.

On the Resource Management 1,000-word continuous speech task, the authors report about a 10% relative error reduction over an already strong continuous-HMM system. Relative reduction means a decrease in the existing error level, not a ten-percentage-point increase in accuracy. The finding supports improving the recognizer through task-directed preprocessing.
neurips-1997-hybrid-nn-hmm-based-speech-.tldr: Neural preprocessing of multiple speech frames improves a continuous-HMM recognizer, yielding about a 10% relative error reduction.

paragraphs: Nystagmus involves slow eye rotations in one direction followed by rapid movements that reset eye position. Periodic alternating nystagmus, or PAN, is an uncontrollable form described as an unstable oscillation whose amplitude remains bounded. The paper investigates how this behavior can arise from the systems that normally regulate eye movement.

The authors report that prolonged rotation in darkness can produce PAN in normal subjects. This observation expands the circumstances associated with the phenomenon, which had previously been observed only in subjects with vestibulo-cerebellar damage. It motivates a model in which abnormal oscillation need not require permanent damage to the relevant control system.

In the proposed explanation, eye-movement circuits are inherently unstable, while the cerebellum normally restrains that instability. Damage or plastic changes caused by rotation in darkness can alter the restraint and allow PAN to appear. The model connects the experimentally induced and damage-associated cases through a shared control mechanism. It also shifts the explanatory focus toward how normal cerebellar regulation keeps unstable dynamics in check.
neurips-1997-instabilities-in-eye-moveme.tldr: PAN induced by rotation in darkness motivates a model in which the cerebellum normally restrains unstable eye-movement circuits.

paragraphs: An overcomplete representation offers more basis vectors than there are input variables, giving a signal more possible building blocks. This flexibility lets the vectors specialize in a wider variety of patterns, but it also creates ambiguity: the same input can have multiple representations. The paper develops a probabilistic learning method that addresses both flexibility and ambiguity.

The model represents data with a linear combination of basis vectors plus additive noise. A Laplacian prior favors sparse coefficients, assigning different probabilities to alternative representations and reducing redundancy. Although reconstruction uses a linear basis, inferring the coefficients becomes a nonlinear function of the input. The authors also improve the approximation used to learn the basis, addressing weaknesses of an earlier approximation at low noise and greater overcompleteness.

The approach generalizes independent component analysis and provides a method for separating more sources than there are mixtures. On natural speech, the learned representations show potentially much greater coding efficiency than a Fourier basis. The stated advantage comes from combining data-adapted features with a probabilistic preference for economical representations.
neurips-1997-learning-nonlinear-overcomp.tldr: A probabilistic algorithm learns overcomplete sparse representations that offer potentially more efficient coding of natural speech.

paragraphs: Data can require many coordinates overall while occupying only a few important directions within a small neighborhood. This paper studies how to exploit that local simplicity before fitting a prediction model. The setting is locally weighted linear regression, where nearby observations receive greater influence on the prediction being made.

The authors derive local forms of several dimensionality-reduction methods: factor analysis regression, principal component regression, principal component regression on joint distributions, and partial least squares regression. Each offers a different statistical route to reducing the variables used in local prediction. Comparing them within the same regression setting makes it possible to ask which assumptions are useful in practice.

Monte Carlo simulations test robustness when the methods' statistical assumptions are violated. Locally weighted partial least squares produces the best average results, outperforming factor analysis despite the latter's theoretical appeal. The finding emphasizes that an attractive statistical model is not enough to determine practical performance. For the examined local regression problems, resilience to assumption violations matters when choosing a reduced representation.
neurips-1997-local-dimensionality-reduct.tldr: Locally weighted partial least squares performs best on average in simulations comparing local dimensionality-reduction methods.

paragraphs: The paper models visual-cell responses during natural viewing, asking how well a classical energy mechanism explains activity and what additional suppression contributes. The full model divides the energy mechanism's output by terms representing nonclassical gain control and texture contrast. This makes the predicted response depend on more than the energy mechanism alone.

The authors use review movies that reproduce the stimulation a cell receives while freely viewing natural images. They collect data from three cells using five review movies and fit the model separately for each movie. This arrangement evaluates the model against temporally changing input related to natural viewing, while allowing each movie's responses to receive their own fit.

The energy mechanism alone yields modest but significant correlations with recorded activity. Adding suppressive surround effects improves the correlations somewhat. In one case, delayed surround suppression substantially improves the fit by changing the predicted response's time course. That result highlights timing as an important part of suppression: its contribution can involve reshaping when a cell responds, beyond adjusting response strength.
neurips-1997-modeling-complex-cells-in-a.tldr: Adding surround suppression improves models of visual-cell responses, with delayed suppression markedly improving one response time course.

paragraphs: Daily rainfall varies with particular weather patterns as well as broader seasonal and long-term changes. This paper proposes a neural-network approach that models the conditional distribution of rainfall amounts. Modeling a distribution describes the range and relative likelihood of possible amounts, giving a richer account of rainfall variation than a single predicted value.

The model determines the order of the process, meaning how much past information is needed to describe its dependence over time. It also determines how the conditional distribution's shape and scale change with time. These are linked aspects of the modeling task: the relevant history and the character of rainfall variability are both inferred within the approach.

The authors then integrate over particular weather patterns to extract seasonal variation and long-term trends. This averaging step connects detailed conditional descriptions with broader temporal behavior. The contribution is a way to move from modeling daily fluctuations to identifying systematic changes, while allowing both the process's memory and its rainfall distributions to be determined by the model.
neurips-1997-modelling-seasonality-and-t.tldr: A neural rainfall model learns temporal dependence and changing distributions, then averages over weather patterns to extract seasons and trends.

paragraphs: Blind source separation seeks to recover underlying signals from observed mixtures. This paper derives a parameter-update rule by examining the geometry of likelihood optimization. Its central choice is to measure distances in parameter space using the Fisher information matrix, which describes how sensitively the modeled distribution changes with the parameters.

With Fisher information serving as the metric, the direction of steepest likelihood improvement is defined by that statistical geometry. The authors show that this construction produces a serial, multiplicative updating rule with an equivariant property. Equivariance expresses a consistent transformation of the algorithm's behavior when the corresponding representation changes. The update is therefore connected to the structure of the statistical problem.

The paper further simplifies the algorithm using the asymptotic form of Fisher information near equilibrium. That qualification matters because the simplification relies on local behavior around that state. The contribution is a derivation connecting a practical form of iterative updating to likelihood and information geometry, together with a route to reducing the update's complexity.
neurips-1997-multiplicative-updating-rul.tldr: Using Fisher information to define optimization geometry yields an equivariant multiplicative update for blind source separation.

paragraphs: Acting toward a particular side of an object requires accounting for where the object is and how it is oriented. This paper presents a neural model that can direct eye movements to the requested side despite changes in position and orientation. It asks what kind of internal representation is sufficient for that behavior.

The model's intermediate units have receptive fields defined relative to the eyes. Their response gain is modulated by the intended side of the object and its orientation. This combination allows eye-centered units to support a task defined relative to an object. The authors report that the gain modulations agree with single-cell recordings from the supplementary eye field.

The same approach also accounts for object-centered neglect, in which patients with a right parietal lesion ignore an object's left side regardless of its orientation. Together, these results show that object-centered behavior and deficits can arise without neurons arranged in an object-centered coordinate map. The model establishes a possible mechanism, separating the reference frame of the task from that of individual receptive fields.
neurips-1997-neural-basis-of-object-cent.tldr: Gain-modulated eye-centered neurons can support object-centered eye movements and account for object-centered neglect.

paragraphs: An extracellular recording can contain waveforms generated by several nearby neurons. Separating those contributions requires describing how waveforms from the same cell vary and distinguishing that variation from differences between cells. This paper frames the task explicitly as probabilistic inference, using models of how individual cells generate their recorded waveforms.

The proposed models contain latent variables: aspects of the generating process that are not directly observed in the recording. Their complexity ranges from a single Gaussian distribution for each cell to a mixture of hidden Markov models. These alternatives offer different levels of detail for describing the distribution of waveforms associated with a cell.

The authors emphasize the common statistical framework rather than prescribing one generative model for every experiment. The model's details can be chosen to match the specific neural preparation. This matters because waveform separation then rests on an explicit account of within-cell variability. It provides a structured way to relate assumptions about recorded signals to the inference of their cellular origins.
neurips-1997-on-the-separation-of-signal.tldr: Probabilistic latent-variable models separate neighboring neurons' waveforms while allowing the signal model to suit the recording preparation.

paragraphs: An auditory system's response to a small change in sound can depend on the sound already present. This paper introduces an m-sequence-based method for measuring that local response while other stimuli, including speech or sinusoidal modulations, continue to play. The goal is to characterize the system under different operating conditions.

The method uses perturbations to estimate a linear response kernel, also described as a receptive field. A kernel summarizes how small stimulus changes relate to response changes around the current operating point. Measuring it during another stimulus makes it possible to study local sensitivity in that context, rather than assuming a single response description applies across all conditions.

The authors apply the method to individual units in the cat's inferior colliculus, calculating modulation transfer functions at different operating points. These functions characterize responses to stimulus modulation. The resulting analysis provides a way to examine nonlinear behavior through context-dependent linear measurements. The paper's methodological contribution is making those measurements possible while the auditory system is receiving other structured stimulation.
neurips-1997-perturbative-m-sequences-fo.tldr: An m-sequence perturbation method measures auditory response kernels while other sounds establish different operating conditions.

paragraphs: This paper brings Bayesian parameter estimation to radial basis function networks. The approach describes uncertainty through a posterior distribution over parameters, rather than retaining only a single fitted setting. The authors develop a Gaussian approximation to that posterior, providing a tractable form for representing the parameters after observing data.

A key condition is that the basis-function widths are fixed. Under that condition, the approximation is analytic in the parameters. This gives the Bayesian treatment a concrete mathematical simplification while making clear which part of the network configuration is held constant. The contribution concerns how to represent and adapt uncertainty within that setting.

The paper also addresses regularization constants, which control the strength of constraints on fitting. It argues that choosing them through cross-validation is wasteful when only one optimal parameter estimate is retained. Instead, the authors assign prior distributions to these constants and adapt them using a simple re-estimation formula. This incorporates regularization selection into the probabilistic treatment and lets the observed data update those choices.
neurips-1997-radial-basis-functions-a-ba.tldr: A Bayesian treatment of radial basis function networks approximates parameter uncertainty and adapts regularization constants from data.

paragraphs: Different learning rules can produce selective responses in a model neuron, but comparisons become difficult when the inputs or architecture also change. This paper holds both fixed: every rule uses the same single-cell architecture and natural-scene environment. That setup focuses the comparison on how the learning rule shapes feature extraction and neural coding.

The rules include skewness maximization, kurtosis maximization, quadratic BCM learning, and single-cell independent component analysis. The authors also use a structure-removal method to investigate which parts of the input distribution influence the learned receptive fields. They find that these receptive fields depend on a small portion of the distribution, giving a more specific account of what drives the resulting selectivity.

When the distribution contains directions with kurtotic structure, quadratic BCM behaves similarly to kurtosis maximization. Its modification equations are computationally simpler, however. This connects a biologically motivated learning rule with a statistical objective under a stated condition. It suggests that similar feature selectivity can arise from learning procedures with different mathematical forms and computational demands.
neurips-1997-receptive-field-formation-i.tldr: Controlled comparisons connect quadratic BCM learning with kurtosis maximization and identify concentrated statistical influences on receptive-field formation.

paragraphs: A communication network must decide which calls to admit and which routes they should use. These decisions share a common objective: making effective use of limited network resources. The paper treats admission and routing as a sequential decision problem, where a choice about one call affects the resources available for subsequent traffic.

Dynamic programming provides a natural formulation, but solving that formulation exactly is too complex for the network considered. The authors instead combine reinforcement learning with a decomposition approach to obtain decision policies. Decomposition breaks the overall problem into more manageable parts, while reinforcement learning supplies a method for learning how to make decisions within that approach.

The policy is evaluated on a network with approximately 10^45 different feature configurations and compared with a commonly used heuristic. The stated scale explains why exact enumeration is impractical and why approximate policy methods are relevant. The abstract establishes the comparison without specifying its outcome. The contribution is the application of learning and decomposition to the coupled resource-allocation decisions.
neurips-1997-reinforcement-learning-for-.tldr: Reinforcement learning and decomposition provide call-admission and routing policies for a network too complex for exact dynamic programming.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning can face a large search space when it must discover an entire policy without structural guidance. This paper constrains the policies under consideration using hierarchies of partially specified machines. The machines encode some organization of behavior while leaving choices open for the learning process to resolve.

This arrangement gives prior knowledge a direct role in determining which solutions the learner explores. The hierarchy also provides a framework for transferring knowledge across problems and recombining component solutions into behavior for larger tasks. The approach connects reinforcement learning with behavior-based and teleo-reactive control by bringing structured descriptions of behavior into policy learning.

The authors present algorithms for both problem-solving and learning with hierarchical machines and prove their convergence. They also demonstrate effectiveness on a problem with several thousand states. The central tradeoff is inherent in the method: the hierarchy reduces the search space by constraining available policies. Its benefit is a way to retain learnable decisions while supplying reusable structure that helps organize a complicated control problem.
neurips-1997-reinforcement-learning-with.tldr: Partially specified hierarchical machines constrain reinforcement learning, enabling structured search and reusable component solutions with convergent algorithms.

paragraphs: Combining several models requires deciding how much weight each should receive. For ordinary averaging under squared error, the error's dependence on these weights motivates quadratic programming. This paper extends that line of reasoning to models whose outputs are probability statements, using a logarithmic opinion pool to combine them.

A logarithmic opinion pool combines predictions through weighted logarithms of probabilities. The authors show that the reasoning connecting model averaging, bias–variance decompositions, and weight optimization applies beyond squared-error models when Kullback–Leibler divergence serves as the error measure. That divergence measures disagreement between probability distributions, allowing the framework to address probabilistic predictions of different kinds.

The paper illustrates the approach with classification models evaluated through cross-entropy and with models that estimate variances. These examples demonstrate the intended breadth of the weighting framework. The contribution is a common statistical rationale for choosing ensemble weights across different prediction tasks. Its stated condition is the use of Kullback–Leibler divergence, which supplies the shared error measure needed for the generalization.
neurips-1997-selecting-weighting-factors.tldr: Logarithmic opinion pools extend ensemble-weight optimization to diverse probabilistic models when error is measured by Kullback–Leibler divergence.

paragraphs: Time-series observations depend on one another, so learning theory for memoryless processes does not directly capture their temporal structure. This paper brings that dependence into a uniform-convergence analysis of prediction. Uniform convergence concerns how reliably performance measured on a finite sample reflects performance across a whole class of candidate predictors.

The authors derive finite-sample bounds expressed through covering numbers of the approximating class. Covering numbers quantify how many representative functions are needed to describe a class at a chosen precision. This connects the richness of the predictor family to the uncertainty involved in estimating its performance from limited, temporally dependent observations.

The analysis addresses the tradeoff between approximation and estimation: richer classes can represent more relationships, but their performance is harder to estimate reliably. The paper outlines complexity regularization based on structural risk minimization and establishes its applicability to mixing stochastic processes. Mixing supplies the relevant dependence setting. The result extends a principled approach to model complexity selection into time-series prediction while explicitly accounting for temporal dependence.
neurips-1997-structural-risk-minimizatio.tldr: Finite-sample learning bounds justify structural risk minimization for time-series prediction under mixing dependence.

paragraphs: Evidence that face recognition and other object recognition can be impaired separately suggests partially independent processing mechanisms. This paper asks whether such specialization must be innately specified. It proposes that competition during learning can allocate neural resources according to the interaction between available visual information and the task being learned.

The authors build a feed-forward model with two modules competing to classify stimuli. In the critical condition, one module receives low spatial frequencies, which convey coarser image structure, while the other receives high spatial frequencies, which convey finer detail. The task requires identifying individual faces while only classifying the other objects.

Under that combination, the low-frequency module develops strong specialization for faces. No other tested combination of tasks and inputs produces the same strong specialization. The finding therefore ties specialization to both the information supplied and the distinctions demanded by the task. The authors interpret this as support for a learned route to face specialization, showing how a dedicated face-processing module need not be specified in advance.
neurips-1997-task-and-spatial-frequency-.tldr: A competitive model develops face specialization through a specific interaction between spatial-frequency inputs and identification demands.

paragraphs: A standard classifier can be used as a component inside a larger classification algorithm. This paper discusses that strategy through plug-in classification techniques, called PaCTs. The classifier inserted into the procedure is the plug-in classifier, or PiC. The distinction separates the underlying prediction method from the surrounding algorithm that turns it into a new classifier.

Examples of possible components include linear discriminant analysis and tree classifiers. The broader technique can therefore operate on established classification methods rather than requiring an entirely new component learner. The abstract notes that methods in this class often deliver large improvements over using one classifier alone, motivating closer examination of how the surrounding procedure contributes.

The paper investigates one such technique and offers motivation for its success. Its explanatory focus is the value created by the plug-in arrangement: classification performance depends on how a learner is used as well as on the learner itself. This provides a way to study improvements at the level of the overall algorithm while retaining a familiar classifier as its component.
neurips-1997-the-error-coding-and-substi.tldr: The paper investigates why embedding a standard classifier within a plug-in classification procedure can improve performance.

paragraphs: Storage capacity describes how much a neural architecture can store in its weights. This paper studies that capacity for a fully connected committee machine as the number of hidden nodes, K, becomes large. The question concerns the architecture's capacity scaling, rather than the performance of a particular training procedure.

The authors analyze the geometry of weight space in relation to the network's internal representations. They then examine the large-K behavior of quantities called order parameters, which summarize aspects of that structure. This route connects capacity to the organization of possible weight configurations and their internal representations.

The resulting leading-order capacity grows in proportion to K times the square root of log K. The result satisfies an existing mathematical bound. By contrast, the replica-symmetric solution from the conventional Gardner approach violates that bound. This comparison gives the geometric analysis a concrete consistency check: its asymptotic prediction respects a constraint that the alternative calculation fails to meet. The stated scaling applies in the large-hidden-layer limit.
neurips-1997-the-storage-capacity-of-a-f.tldr: A geometric analysis finds large-K committee-machine capacity proportional to K√log K, consistent with an existing mathematical bound.

paragraphs: This paper develops a multilayer perceptron to help distinguish benign from malignant ovarian tumors before surgery. The classifier uses objective observations, including ultrasound morphology, color Doppler imaging, and serum tumor markers. Its purpose is to combine these measurements into a prediction relevant to preoperative assessment.

The authors emphasize that mean squared classification error does not adequately characterize performance for this task. They instead examine sensitivity and specificity, which describe detection of malignant cases and correct recognition of benign cases. Receiver operating characteristic curves combine these considerations, showing how the balance changes as the decision threshold varies.

The network is reported to make reliable predictions with discrimination comparable to that of experienced gynecologists. This concerns its ability to distinguish the two tumor categories. The paper's contribution includes both the classifier and the choice of evaluation framework: assessing a diagnostic model requires examining the types of decisions it makes, rather than relying only on a single averaged numerical error. The measurements and evaluation are tied to the preoperative classification problem.
neurips-1997-use-of-a-multi-layer-percep.tldr: A neural classifier combines preoperative tumor measurements and achieves discrimination reported as comparable to experienced gynecologists.
